newsitem.title: FRANCE: France urges more investment in southeast Asia.
newsitem.headline: France urges more investment in southeast Asia.

text.p: Industry Minister Franck Borotra urged French companies on Tuesday to boost their presence in the rapidly growing economies of southeast Asia to catch up with a more aggressive drive by their Japanese and U.S. counterparts.
The ministry said in a statement that France trails not only Japan and the United States in proportional direct investment to southeast Asia but also Britain and Germany.
Borotra's call came just as France and South Korea are trying to ease tensions fired up by the suspension last week of the privatisation of electronics group Thomson SA.

The Paris government halted the deal after the independent privatisation commission objected to the terms of the proposed sale of Thomson Multimedia to Daewoo Electronics, prompting angry queries from Daewoo and the Korean government.
A Daewoo spokesman in Seoul said the chairman was in Paris on Tuesday to discuss a Thomson deal after France moved to mollify the Koreans by explaining its privatisation process.
The French industry ministry did not refer to the Thomson deal but outlined a string of what it called "worrisome" statistics.

Some of the figures, it said, reflected a general European trend. "While Japan and the United States have made Asia a priority in recent years, the European Union hasn't sufficiently re-oriented its export effort toward this zone," it said.
European exports of manufactured goods to southeast Asia represent six percent of the total, compared with 31 percent for Japan.

In other areas, France lags its European neighbours. French direct investment in the region comprising China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, South Korea, Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines has risen to three percent from one percent in 1985.

In contrast, U.S. direct investment in the region has jumped to 24 percent from one percent over the 10-year period, Japanese investment has doubled to 24 percent from 12 percent, and German investment has risen to nine percent from two percent.
British direct investment in southeast Asia also comes to nine percent of the total and Italian investment to six percent, the statement said.
"Franck Borotra wants to encourage a spirit of conquest and boldness in French industrial firms in regard to this region," it said, citing the growth of a substantial Asian middle class.
"Ten percent of the population has attained western buying power levels, representing a market equivalent to all of Europe," it said.
